name: Papyrus sheet
kb: Cut, layered and pressed papyrus strips
note: Papyrus does not cure; it works wet. The real invention is understanding that plant laminae naturally adhere without paste if pressed fresh.

name: Parchment sheet
kb: Treated animal skin, erasable
note: Scraped skin accepts ink and erasure. The invention is the alkali lime wash to remove hair without destroying fibre.

name: Rag paper sheet
kb: Rag pulp made into sheets by felting
note: China's invention: pulp beaten finer and finer until felts into a sheet on a screen, without pressing to hardness.

name: Quill pen
kb: Sharpened feather barrel with split nib
note: The split must hold capillary action. Quills need re-splitting and re-hardening every few hours.

name: Steel pen nib
kb: Stamped and hardened steel point with slit
note: Stamping gives consistency; hardening to spring temper is critical. Mass production beats labour-intensive quill sharpening.

name: Fountain pen
kb: Sealed ink reservoir with capillary feed and nib
note: The feed must regulate flow by capillary action against air pressure as level drops, without flooding. Took decades to solve.

name: Graphite pencil
kb: Graphite rod graded by clay mix and kiln-fired in clay jacket
note: Graphite hardens in proportion to clay; the German recipe ratios and kiln control took centuries to perfect. Wood jacket came later.

name: Carbon paper
kb: Thin paper coated with carbon black and wax, ink transfers by pressure
note: Coating must be even without clogging the pores. Wax carrier keeps carbon from smudging before use.

name: Iron gall ink
kb: Ferric sulfate from oak galls and copperas, bound in gum arabic
note: The tannin in galls binds iron to cellulose chemically, not just sitting on it. This is why medieval manuscripts survive.

name: Aniline dye ink
kb: Synthetic organic dyes dissolved in water or solvent
note: Aniline inks are brilliant but fade faster than iron gall. They do not chemically bind fibre.

name: Printing ink, oil-based
kb: Linseed oil with carbon black, boiled with resin
note: Oil and resin must polymerise by oxidation without skinning in the pot. The press hardens it by heating, not evaporation.

name: Woodblock printing
kb: Image relief-cut into wood, inked and pressed onto paper
note: Chinese invention: carving a mirror image freehand in wood requires skill. The hardest part is cutting fine lines that do not splinter.

name: Movable type, cast metal
kb: Individual metal letters cast to uniform body height and set into lines
note: Gutenberg's invention was not type, but the punch, matrix and adjustable mould that cast thousands of identical letters to the same body height.

name: Punch and matrix for type
kb: Hardened steel punch strikes soft brass matrix; matrix used to cast type
note: A single punch makes many matrices; each matrix must be struck vertically and squared. The precision is the barrier.

name: Adjustable type mould
kb: Split brass mould with adjustable width, opens to eject cast letter
note: Width must adjust to cast all letters to the same body height. Ejection mechanism must not deform cooling metal.

name: Type metal alloy
kb: Lead-tin-antimony alloy with low melting point and high hardness
note: Lead alone is too soft; tin raises hardness but tin is expensive. Antimony prevents it from shrinking as it cools.

name: Composing stick
kb: Adjustable metal holder for arranging individual type letters into lines
note: Width adjusts to accommodate justified lines of varying length. The spring catch holds letters without crushing them.

name: Chase and forme
kb: Iron frame holding type locked into plane surface by wooden and metal furniture
note: Type must be locked so tightly that quoins cannot shift under press pressure. Wood swells; metal wedges must be wedged, not glued.

name: Screw press for printing
kb: Large wooden frame with screw applying direct downward pressure to platen
note: Screw threads must be clean or they strip. Parallel guides prevent binding. Operator arm length trades speed for force.

name: Iron hand press
kb: All-iron screw press with toggle linkage, much stronger than wooden
note: Cast iron is brittle but strong in compression. Toggle linkage multiplies force near the end of platen travel. Speed rises from hand pressure.

name: Cylinder press
kb: Paper fed between rotating cylinder and flat type bed, steam-driven
note: Cylinder is harder to ink evenly than platen. But feed is continuous; impression is constant at low pressure. Speed rises ten-fold.

name: Rotary press
kb: Type or stereotypes on rotating cylinder, paper fed between cylinders, steam-driven
note: Cylinders must be perfectly parallel and run at constant speed. Register is critical; misalignment ruins thousands of sheets.

name: Stereotype plate
kb: Papier-mache mould of type forme, cast into metal plate, allows curved mounting
note: Papier-mache matrix captures exact impression; the pour must be fast before it cools. Curved plates enable rotary presses.

name: Electrotype plate
kb: Electroplated copper shell backed with lead, captures type forme detail
note: Copper deposits slowly and must be backed by lead to prevent buckling. Thinner backing than stereotype makes faster presses possible.

name: Linotype machine
kb: Keyboard-driven machine that casts entire lines of type as single metal slugs
note: A single operator replaces six hand compositors. Matrices fall from magazines into assembler, then into caster. Slugs are justified and cast molten.

name: Monotype machine
kb: Keyboard punches paper tape, second stage casts individual type from matrices and tape
note: More flexible than Linotype because it casts individual types. Takes more time but allows different sizes on same page without reset.

name: Lithography
kb: Greasy image drawn on limestone, dampened and rolled with oily ink; ink sticks only to image
note: The chemistry is water and grease repellency; limestone's porous structure holds both. Lithographic limestone from Bavaria is irreplaceable.

name: Chromolithography
kb: Separate limestone plate for each colour, each dampened and rolled sequentially
note: Registration between plates must be accurate to fraction of millimetre. Hand-drawn art is required for each colour; masking colour-by-colour.

name: Offset lithography
kb: Lithographic image offset onto rubber blanket, then onto paper, allowing curved or small presses
note: Rubber blanket is expensive but does not damage the stone. Pressure halves because blanket yields. Image reverses twice and comes out correct.

name: Halftone screen and dot matrix
kb: Ruled glass screen creates regular dots from continuous tone photograph
note: Screen must be precision-ruled and at precise angle to metal halftone plate; misalignment causes moiré. Dot size encodes tone.

name: Photoengraving (relief)
kb: Photo-hardened metal resist etched away leaving relief image
note: Photo-resist captures halftone dots; acid etches between them. Relief height must be uniform or ink transfer is patchy.

name: Rotogravure
kb: Etched or electroplated intaglio cylinder, ink wiped from surface, leaving ink in wells of varying depth
note: Well depth encodes tone, not dot size. Ink transfer is continuous not half-tone. Requires high precision wiping blade.

name: Colour separation
kb: Photograph separated through filters into CMYK halftone plates for four-colour printing
note: Red, green, blue filters separate ink into cyan, magenta, yellow, black. Registration between plates must be perfect.

name: Typewriter
kb: Keyboard-driven machine that stamps type bars onto paper through ribbon
note: QWERTY layout prevents type bars from jamming. Shift key mechanism redirects entire basket of type down one notch. Springs must return bars fast.

name: Shift key mechanism
kb: Lever mechanism that moves entire basket of type up or down to produce capitals
note: Shift basket must move reliably without sticking. Spring return must be precise or next keystroke misses. Cam followers are critical.

name: Typewriter ribbon
kb: Inked fabric ribbon that spools past type bars, advances with each strike
note: Ink must not dry out but must not bleed sideways. Spool mechanism must grip and release fabric precisely without stretching it.

name: Stencil duplicator
kb: Typewriter cuts holes in nitrocellulose stencil; stencil stretched across drum, ink pushed through via brush
note: Stencil support screen must hold fabric taut or ink pools. Register sprockets prevent paper misalignment. 200 copies maximum before wear.

name: Mimeograph
kb: Motorised stencil duplicator with spring-driven ink drum rotating against stencil
note: Rotating drum distributes ink evenly; speed is continuous not hand-driven. Stencil wears faster but production runs extend from 200 to 2000.

name: Hectograph
kb: Gelatin pad saturated with glycerol holds aniline-dye master image; paper pressed onto pad picks up image
note: Glycerol prevents gelatin from drying. Image fades with each pull because dye diffuses into gelatin. Up to 100 copies before unusable.

name: Case binding
kb: Sewn signatures glued to raised bands; boards covered with leather or cloth attached to cover with endpapers
note: Signature sewing is essential for durability; gluing alone fails in years. Raised bands protect sewing from shearing when spine flexes.

name: Camera obscura with lens
kb: Darkened box or room with lens projecting inverted image onto screen or ground glass
note: The lens must be good or image is dim. Pinhole works but is too dim for anything but bright sunlight. Artists trace images.

name: Camera lucida
kb: Prism device that superimposes virtual image of subject onto paper at eye, allowing drawing from sight
note: Prism angle must be exactly 45 degrees or optical axis is wrong. Artist traces subject outline, adding shading freehand.

name: Silver halide photographic sensitivity
kb: Silver chloride, bromide or iodide darkens when exposed to light, basis of all photography
note: Light breaks silver halide crystals to silver metal; unexposed crystals must be removed without darkening the image. All photo systems depend on this.

name: Daguerreotype plate
kb: Polished copper plate coated with silver, sensitised with iodine vapour, exposed and developed with mercury vapour
note: Mercury development amalgamates with silver, forming mirror-like image. Irreversible; plates cannot be copied. Each is one-off.

name: Calotype paper negative
kb: Silver iodide emulsion on paper; negative exposed and developed, then contact-printed onto fresh paper to make copies
note: Negative allows unlimited prints. Paper texture shows in final image. Toning with gold chloride prevents fading.

name: Wet collodion plate
kb: Nitrocellulose emulsion on glass, sensitised with silver nitrate, must be exposed and developed wet
note: Sharp, repeatable glass substrate beats paper. Emulsion must stay wet or sensitivity drops. Field photographers carried dark tents.

name: Dry gelatin emulsion plate
kb: Gelatin emulsion on glass that can be dried and stored, remains sensitive for months
note: Gelatin is permeable to silver nitrate after heating. Drying stops reaction but sensitivity remains. Allows casual photographers, not just wet-tent professionals.

name: Celluloid roll film
kb: Gelatin emulsion coated on transparent celluloid film in rolls, spool-fed through camera back
note: Transparent backing allows frame spacing with sprocket holes. Rolls hold 20 to 120 frames. Enables hand-held cameras and amateur photography.

name: Safety film (cellulose acetate)
kb: Cellulose acetate film instead of nitrocellulose, same sensitivity but much safer against fire
note: Nitrocellulose burns like gunpowder; nitrate film archives are fire hazards. Acetate burns but does not support combustion. Cost is higher.

name: Photographic developer
kb: Reducing agents such as pyrogallic acid or hydroquinone that convert exposed silver halide to metallic silver
note: Pyrogallic acid is fast but fades in light; hydroquinone is slower but stable. Alkali pH needed or development fails. Timing is critical.

name: Photographic fixer
kb: Sodium thiosulfate dissolves unexposed silver halide, stopping development and stabilising image
note: Sodium thiosulfate complexes silver halide so it washes away. Without fixing, remaining halide darkens in light. Thorough washing essential.

name: Photographic enlarger
kb: Light source shines through negative, lens projects magnified image onto enlarging paper
note: Condenser system must concentrate light evenly. Negative and lens must focus with precision. Foot and height adjustment critical.

name: Panchromatic emulsion
kb: Gelatin emulsion sensitised to all colours by added dyes, records red green and blue nearly equally
note: Orthochromatic sees only blue and green, rendering reds as black. Panchromatic needs red safelight in darkroom, not yellow.

name: Autochrome colour plate
kb: Glass plate coated with tiny starch grains dyed red, green, blue, gaps filled with carbon black, one panchromatic emulsion layer
note: Viewing requires backlighting. Grains are tiny; resolution is 100 lines per mm. Colours are pastel. Only colour photo process before Kodachrome.

name: Subtractive colour film
kb: Multilayer emulsion with cyan, magenta, yellow layers, each sensitive to different colour; dyes form during development
note: Three-layer coating is precise. Each layer develops in situ without bleaching others. Kodachrome (1935) reversal process; Technicolor uses three strip cameras.

name: Flash powder
kb: Mixture of magnesium powder and potassium perchlorate that burns with intense white light when ignited
note: Magnesium produces blue-white light nearer to daylight than gas flames. Flash burns in fraction of second; exposure still needs 1 second.

name: Flashbulb
kb: Magnesium wire in oxygen-filled bulb, ignited by electrical filament, provides reliable timed flash
note: Oxygen must be pure and bulb sealed; any leak ruins it. One-use; burnout shows through glass when spent. Shutter speed rises to 1/500.

name: Leaf shutter
kb: Overlapping metal blades that open and close radially, allowing flash sync at all speeds
note: Blades must open fully then close evenly. Timing via escapement gears. Flash fires when shutter fully open, works at all exposure times.

name: Focal plane shutter
kb: Cloth or metal curtain that travels across film plane just in front of film, slit width controls exposure time
note: Exposure time set by curtain slit width. Fast speeds only work if slit is very narrow. High speeds above 1/500 require multiple slits.

name: Light meter
kb: Selenium cell generates voltage in proportion to light; meter dial shows film exposure value
note: Selenium cell needs no battery, generates its own current. Sensitive mainly to green light. Averaging across scene is guess-work.

name: Cine camera
kb: Camera that exposes successive film frames at standard rate, records motion on film
note: Intermittent sprocket movement must be reliable and repeatable. Spring or motor drive. Hand-crank adds fatigue; motor steadier.

name: Intermittent film movement (Maltese cross)
kb: Rotating Maltese cross cam drives film advance pin intermittently, pausing for exposure
note: Cross slots must be precise or pin binds. Motion is smooth during pull-down, allowing high speed without shaking film.

name: Film projector
kb: Light source, lens and intermittent film advance project enlarged image at standard frame rate
note: Shutter must blank lens during pull-down to prevent flicker. Gate must hold film flat. Heat dissipation critical with arc lamp.

name: Animation cel
kb: Transparent celluloid sheet with hand-drawn animation character ink and paint, photographed over painted background
note: Cel movement is stop-frame photography; each frame is separate drawing. Inking and painting must be consistent across thousands of cels.

name: Phonautograph
kb: Sound vibrations move stylus that traces wavy line onto soot-covered cylinder
note: Records sound into grooves but cannot play back. Stylus must be rigid enough to not break but flexible enough to move. Soot captures trace.

name: Tin foil phonograph
kb: Tinfoil-covered cylinder, stylus indents foil during recording, same stylus reproduces sound by following groove
note: Tinfoil indents rather than cuts; playback is faint. Surface crinkles after 10-20 plays. Cylinder speed must be exactly repeatable.

name: Wax cylinder record
kb: Removable cylinder of hardened wax, stylus indents grooves during recording, springs back slightly on playback
note: Wax gives 100+ plays. Cylinders can be shaved and recoated for reuse. Playback volume limited; needle vibrates wax, not driven by it.

name: Disc record
kb: Flat shellac disc with spiral groove cut by rotating stylus, mass-produced by pressing from metal matrix
note: Disc format allows mass production. 78 RPM is standard. Shellac is fragile; discs shatter on impact. Playback by needle vibration.

name: Lateral-cut groove
kb: Spiral groove is cut left-right (lateral), not up-down; stylus traces groove wall vibrations
note: Lateral eliminates surface noise from needle pressure. Groove walls must be cut at precise angle or tracking is poor.

name: Acoustic horn recording
kb: Sound collected by horn, focused onto diaphragm with stylus, no electrical amplification
note: Horn gains is logarithmic; tighter curve amplifies more. Frequency response is lumpy; bass is absent. Diaphragm compliance limits stylus force.

name: Gramophone motor and governor
kb: Spring-driven or electric motor with centrifugal governor that maintains constant disc speed
note: Speed variation ruins pitch fidelity. Centrifugal governor adjusts throttle; electrical governors use rheostats. Flywheel smooths spring torque ripple.

name: Carbon microphone
kb: Sound vibrations change electrical resistance of carbon-packed diaphragm, modulates current in circuit
note: Carbon packing pressure is critical; too loose and sensitivity drops, too tight and resistance is constant. Short lifetime; packing settles.

name: Moving coil microphone
kb: Diaphragm drives coil suspended in permanent magnet field, motion generates voltage in coil
note: Coil impedance is low; step-up transformer needed. Frequency response is smooth. Output level is low compared to carbon.

name: Condenser microphone
kb: Diaphragm is one plate of capacitor, vibration changes capacitance, voltage across capacitor varies
note: Requires high voltage bias and impedance converter. Flat frequency response and high sensitivity. Fragile and temperature sensitive.

name: Moving coil loudspeaker driver
kb: Coil suspended in magnet field carries audio current, drives paper cone attached to voice coil former
note: Paper cone is resonant; large speaker sizes smooth response. Impedance 4-16 ohms. Magnet must be strong and free of stray fields.

name: Magnetic wire recording
kb: Steel wire magnetised by AC bias current modulated by audio signal, playback coil detects magnetic state
note: Tape speed and bias frequency are critical. Erase head removes prior recording before recording head. Wire is fragile and tangles.

name: Magnetic tape recording
kb: Paper backing coated with iron oxide particles, magnetised by AC bias, tape spools smoothly through transport
note: Tape allows high speed and long storage. Oxide particles must be fine and uniform. Tape stretches and must be tensioned carefully.

name: AC bias for tape recording
kb: High-frequency AC signal applied to recording head along with audio signal, linearises magnetisation
note: Without bias, record-playback distortion is severe. Bias frequency above 20 kHz. Bias level is critical; too little and distortion rises.

name: Disc cutting lathe
kb: Lathe with precision spindle, variable speed, feeds stylus into rotating wax master disc
note: Spiral feed pitch must be precise or groove spacing varies. Speed must be constant or pitch wavers. Stylus wear must be compensated.

name: Record pressing and moulding
kb: Metal matrices from masters pressed into hot shellac compound under hydraulic pressure, cools and releases finished disc
note: Shellac temperature and pressure are critical; too hot and it flows sideways, too cold and voids form. Hydraulic power is essential.

name: Stereophony
kb: Two independent audio channels recorded separately, played back through two speakers
note: Stereo requires two grooves or two tracks. Disc sterics uses lateral and vertical modulation on same groove. Channel separation is critical.

name: Electric telegraph
kb: Key switch closes electromagnet circuit, solenoid pulls armature clicking against stop, audible signal transmits over wire
note: Single needle telegraph precedes it; this is sounder-based. Relay allows weak signal to switch strong signal at repeater.

name: Morse key and sounder
kb: Standardised key for sending dots and dashes, sounder produces distinctive click for each pulse
note: Morse code uses short and long pulses. Sounder design affects learning; American style fast and bright, German style slower.

name: Telegraph relay
kb: Weak signal closes electromagnet, switching separate high-power circuit for long-distance repeating
note: Allows unlimited range; weak local battery switches strong line battery. Contacts must be clean or arc burns them.

name: Submarine cable with gutta percha
kb: Copper conductor insulated with gutta percha tropical rubber, coated with protective jute or iron wire, laid on ocean floor
note: Gutta percha is only usable insulator waterproof enough; unavailable locally. Requires tropical expedition to acquire. Laying is hazardous.

name: Cable repeater and amplifier
kb: Relay chain that regenerates telegraph pulses, extends cable distance from 100 km to 1000+ km
note: Repeater senses weak signal, switches local battery. Critical for intercontinental cables. Submerged repeaters are hard to maintain.

name: Telephone transmitter (microphone)
kb: Sound-modulated current; carbon granule transmitter has poor fidelity but high gain
note: Carbon transmitter is louder than mouth against open mouthpiece but prone to feedback. Requires constant voltage supply.

name: Telephone receiver (earphone)
kb: Coil on permanent magnet vibrates armature against diaphragm, converts current to sound
note: Fidelity poor; frequencies outside 300-3400 Hz are lost. Impedance must match handset coil. Diaphragm vibration is violent but amplitude small.

name: Telephone exchange and switchboard
kb: Manual exchange where operators patch telephone lines between calling and called subscribers
note: Operator hears both parties; must avoid feedback. Bank of jacks and cords. Switchboard capacity limited to operators available.

name: Strowger automatic exchange
kb: Dial pulses rotate stepping switch across multiple levels, selecting destination line without operator
note: Stepping switches are electromechanical selectors. Wipers must move vertically and rotate horizontally. Bearing wear is rapid.

name: Loading coil (Pupinisation)
kb: Inductance coil added to telephone line at intervals, reduces attenuation of high frequencies, extends range
note: Loading periodically spaced; wrong spacing causes new problems. Increases range from 20 to 50 km on single pair. Crosstalk increases.

name: Spark transmitter
kb: High-voltage spark across gap generates radio waves in tuned LC circuit
note: Spark gap must erode uniformly; motor-driven rotation prevents pitting. Emission is damped wave; bandwidth very wide.

name: Coherer detector
kb: Glass tube with metal filings in loose contact; radio wave ionises air, filings cohere and reduce resistance
note: Cohering is not instantaneous; filings lag received wave. Decohering is slow; requires tapping to shake loose again.

name: Crystal detector
kb: Galena or similar mineral crystal at point-contact; point acts as rectifier, demodulates radio wave
note: Cat's whisker point must be pressed precisely; detector is temperamental. Much more reliable than coherer. Requires no power.

name: Tuned LC circuit
kb: Inductor and capacitor in series or parallel; resonance at specific frequency, amplifies that frequency
note: Resonance is sharpest with low resistance; high Q demands low loss. Variable capacitor tunes frequency across band.

name: Continuous wave transmitter
kb: Vacuum tube or alternator generates continuous sinusoidal wave, modulated by Morse key
note: CW is narrower bandwidth than spark. Regenerative circuits required to maintain frequency stability. Frequency drift is problem.

name: Alexanderson alternator
kb: High-speed alternator with many poles and laminated rotor, generates stable RF continuously, 50-500 kHz
note: Synchronous rectifier is required for conversion. Stability allows world-wide ship-to-shore wireless. Superseded by vacuum tube transmitters.

name: Triode oscillator
kb: Vacuum triode in feedback oscillator circuit generates stable continuous wave at tuned frequency
note: Feedback coupling must be precise; too much causes chirping, too little lacks output. Better frequency stability than alternator.

name: Amplitude modulation (AM)
kb: Audio signal varies amplitude of radio carrier wave, bandwidth twice the audio frequency
note: Audio is mixed with carrier before transmission. Receiver rectifies and filters to recover audio. Atmospheric noise is also amplitude-modulated.

name: Superheterodyne receiver
kb: Local oscillator beats with received signal, produces intermediate frequency easily amplified and filtered
note: IF frequency stays fixed; tuning shifts oscillator, not RF amplifier. Single-tuned dial is huge improvement. Image response is problem.

name: Frequency modulation (FM)
kb: Audio signal varies frequency of radio carrier, bandwidth depends on modulation index, immune to amplitude noise
note: Wider bandwidth than AM. Receiver requires frequency limiter and discriminator. More complex but noise floor lower.

name: Dipole antenna
kb: Two metal rods half-wavelength apart, high impedance at resonance, couples RF to space
note: Radiation resistance is low; matching is essential. Overhead antenna is key; ground connection less important than height.

name: Radio direction finding (RDF)
kb: Loop antenna rotated to find null or maximum signal, determines bearing to transmitter
note: Null is sharper than maximum; bearing error is few degrees. Two RDFs triangulate position. Used for ship navigation and enemy location.

name: Radar
kb: Pulse transmitter and receiver with CRT display, shows range and bearing to reflective objects
note: Pulse repetition rate and receiver timing must be precise. CRT displays radar return. Critical for detecting aircraft. Extremely difficult.

name: Cathode ray tube
kb: Electron beam from cathode accelerated and deflected by electric or magnetic fields, writes image on fluorescent screen
note: Deflection coils must be perfectly symmetrical. Phosphor screen degrades with use. Vacuum must be very good or electrons are scattered.

name: Television by mechanical scanning
kb: Rotating disc with scanning holes moves image spot across photoelectric cell, electrical signal transmitted
note: Disc must rotate precisely; flicker is problem at low frame rates. Extremely dim; receiver needs very good amplification.

name: Iconoscope camera tube
kb: Electron beam scans photoelectric mosaic target, each cell's charge varies with light, produces video signal
note: Mosaic target must have fine structure; silver-cesium oxide cells used. Capacitive coupling to each cell is critical.

name: Image orthicon tube
kb: Photocathode converts image to electrons, electron beam reads them, sensitive 100x iconoscope
note: Photocathode is vacuum deposited. Internal electron multiplication by impact ionisation. Sensitive enough for broadcasting.

name: Video scanning standard (NTSC or PAL)
kb: Agreed frame rate, lines per frame, timing of sync pulses, allows all cameras and receivers to interoperate
note: Frame rate matched to power line frequency (60 Hz US, 50 Hz Europe). Sync timing allows receiver to lock. Adoption is slow.

name: Facsimile transmission
kb: Document scanned by rotating drum, light and dark areas modulate radio frequency, transmitted over telephone line
note: Synchronisation between sender and receiver must be perfect or image skews. Scanning speed trades resolution for transmission time.

name: Punched card
kb: Paper card with holes representing data, mechanically read by sensing pins or brushes
note: Card format is 80 columns, 12 rows; de facto standard. Holes are read by mechanically sensing gaps.

name: Jacquard card chain
kb: Chain of linked punched cards describing repeating pattern, threaded through loom to control thread selection
note: Card-driven loom reduces pattern complexity from artisan memorisation. Thousands of cards weave complex fabrics. Precursor to digital computing.

name: Hollerith tabulator
kb: Electrical device reads punched cards, counts and tabulates data automatically
note: Tabulating machine uses reading brushes that sense hole positions. Mechanical counters advance. Census processing time falls from years to weeks.

name: Card sorter
kb: Machine reads punched card, electromagnet actuates solenoid directing card into appropriate bin
note: Solenoid plunger must be fast and strong. Cards must not jam. Sorting falls to seconds per card from manual tedium.

name: Keypunch machine
kb: Typewriter-like keyboard, each key strikes punch that pierces corresponding hole in card
note: Card must be held precisely during punch. Operator verifies key before strike. Jams are common; need sturdy card stock.

name: Adding machine
kb: Mechanical calculator with keyboard, numbers entered, crank turned, sum appears in window
note: Carry mechanism is critical; each decade must propagate carry to next. Segmented drums rotate to display numbers. Addition only, not multiplication.

name: Comptometer
kb: Ten keys per column, ten columns, touch keys in sequence without using crank, result shown continuously
note: Continuous operation; touching key advances number. Multiplication by repeated addition. Faster than crank machines once mastered.

name: Cash register
kb: Register totals sale amount, opens drawer, prints receipt, bell rings, records transaction mechanically
note: Mechanical register prevents underring. Solenoid locks drawer. Receipt paper roll hidden. Counter records every transaction.

name: Slide rule
kb: Two logarithmic scales, one sliding past the other, performs multiplication and division by adding lengths
note: Accuracy limited by cursor precision. Mantissa is entered manually. Exponent tracked separately. Requires training.

name: Difference engine
kb: Mechanical calculator using method of differences, produces mathematical tables by pure mechanism
note: Babbage's design; never fully completed in his time. Requires perfect tolerance; carry is difficult. Generates error-free tables once built.

name: Teletype paper tape
kb: Narrow paper tape with holes representing typed characters, machine-readable for retransmission or storage
note: Narrow tape (1 inch) uses 5 or 8 hole format. Perforated by typewriter keyboard action. Telegraph signals re-read tape.

name: Microfilm and microcard
kb: Pages photographed at high magnification on film or card, stored compactly, projected or enlarged for reading
note: Reduction ratio is 10-100x. Reader must have objective lens and screen. Archival storage is compact.

name: Index card and filing system
kb: Uniform sized cards with alphabetic or numeric index allow rapid retrieval of categorised information
note: 3 by 5 inch card is standard. Filing order discipline is essential. Allows ad-hoc rearrangement; improvement over bound ledgers.

name: Dewey decimal classification
kb: Hierarchical decimal numbering system allowing any topic to be assigned unique number enabling shelf ordering
note: System is hierarchical; all zeros are philosophy, hundreds are pure sciences. Allows insertion of new topics without renumbering.
